name: Mezzotint
basis: why: plate roughened to print black, then burnished toward light; how: ink where darkness beats plate roughness, plate mark
note: Intaglio, kept apart from line engraving because tone comes from pits, not lines.

lumenary.blurb: A copper plate roughened all over so it prints velvet black, then burnished smooth wherever the picture is light.

facts.era: Invented in 1642, popular in 17th to 19th century Europe
facts.bestOn: Dark, moody pictures with soft light

why: Mezzotint begins with darkness and works towards light. A copper plate is roughened evenly with a toothed tool so that it holds ink as a dense field of pits and prints solid black. The engraver then burnishes the plate smooth where the picture should be lighter, and smoother copper holds less ink, so tone is made from the density of tiny pits instead of lines or dots.
how: Make a random value for each point, a mix of 62 percent white noise per grain cell and 38 percent smooth noise, to stand for the plate’s roughness.
Raise the picture’s darkness to a power set by the burnishing slider.
Ink the pixel where darkness beats the roughness, softening the decision with a smoothstep of width plus or minus 0.1.
Dark areas win almost everywhere and print black. Light areas win only at the roughest pits and stay mostly white with scattered specks.
Add a bevelled plate mark where the plate pressed into the paper.
history: The method is credited to Ludwig von Siegen, a German officer, in 1642, and Prince Rupert of the Rhine introduced it to England. In the eighteenth century it became the English favourite for reproducing portraits and paintings, valued for its velvety darks, before photography replaced it.
uses: Dramatic portrait and still life prints
Book plates and fine art reproductions
terms: A toothed, curved tool rocked across a plate to roughen it.
A smooth tool used to polish areas of the plate so they hold less ink.
The dent a plate leaves around a print.
paragraphs: Mezzotint begins with a copper plate roughened all over with a rocker, so that it holds ink as a dense field of pits and prints solid black. The engraver then burnishes the plate smooth where the picture should be lighter; smoother copper holds less ink. Tone is therefore made from the density of tiny pits, not from lines or dots.

The program does the same in reverse. A random value, a mix of 62% white noise (per grain cell) and 38% smooth noise, stands for how rough the plate is at each point. Darkness is raised to a power (the burnishing slider controls how much) and compared with that value: where darkness wins, the pixel takes ink, softened by a smoothstep of width ±0.1. Dark areas win nearly everywhere and are black; light areas win only at the roughest pits and stay white with scattered black specks, which is exactly the velvet gradation of the original. A bevelled edge shows where the plate pressed into the paper.

equations.note: Darkness after burnishing b (0 to 1), and the roughness n of the plate (r white noise per grain cell, ν smooth noise).
Ink coverage a at a pixel.

presets.text: Heavy burnishing gives bright highlights on a deep ground.
Sepia ink with coarse grain feels antique.
Hide the plate mark to fill the page.
